claim: Hundreds of human genes are associated with neurological diseases.
source: Hundreds of human genes are associated with neurological diseases, but translation into tractable biological mechanisms is lagging.
evidence: This is a general statement about the current state of genomic research in neurological diseases, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Translation of gene-disease associations into tractable biological mechanisms is lagging.
source: Hundreds of human genes are associated with neurological diseases, but translation into tractable biological mechanisms is lagging.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of the field and the motivation for the study.

claim: Larval zebrafish are an attractive model to investigate genetic contributions to neurological diseases.
source: Larval zebrafish are an attractive model to investigate genetic contributions to neurological diseases.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism and is further supported by citations in the Introduction.

claim: Current CRISPR-Cas9 methods are difficult to apply to large genetic screens studying behavioural phenotypes.
source: However, current CRISPR-Cas9 methods are difficult to apply to large genetic screens studying behavioural phenotypes.
evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of existing methods and represents a gap in the field that motivates their work.

claim: The authors developed a simple sequencing-free tool to validate gRNAs.
source: To facilitate rapid genetic screening, we developed a simple sequencing-free tool to validate gRNAs and a highly effective CRISPR-Cas9 method capable of converting >90% of injected embryos directly into F0 biallelic knockouts.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The authors developed a CRISPR-Cas9 method capable of converting >90% of injected embryos directly into F0 biallelic knockouts.
source: To facilitate rapid genetic screening, we developed a simple sequencing-free tool to validate gRNAs and a highly effective CRISPR-Cas9 method capable of converting >90% of injected embryos directly into F0 biallelic knockouts.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate complex mutant phenotypes including altered molecular rhythms of the circadian clock.
source: We demonstrate that F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate complex mutant phenotypes, such as altered molecular rhythms of the circadian clock, escape responses to irritants, and multi-parameter day-night locomotor behaviours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B showing circadian rhythm phenotypes in csnk1db F0 knockouts.

claim: F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate escape responses to irritants.
source: We demonstrate that F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate complex mutant phenotypes, such as altered molecular rhythms of the circadian clock, escape responses to irritants, and multi-parameter day-night locomotor behaviours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A showing trpa1b F0 knockout response to mustard oil.

claim: F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate multi-parameter day-night locomotor behaviours.
source: We demonstrate that F0 knockouts reliably recapitulate complex mutant phenotypes, such as altered molecular rhythms of the circadian clock, escape responses to irritants, and multi-parameter day-night locomotor behaviours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6 showing scn1lab F0 knockout behavioral phenotypes.

claim: The F0 knockout technique is sufficiently robust to knockout multiple genes in the same animal.
source: The technique is sufficiently robust to knockout multiple genes in the same animal, for example to create the transparent triple knockout crystal fish for imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing double and triple gene knockouts.

claim: The F0 knockout method cuts the experimental time from gene to behavioural phenotype in zebrafish from months to one week.
source: Our F0 knockout method cuts the experimental time from gene to behavioural phenotype in zebrafish from months to one week.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between traditional breeding methods (which take 4-6 months) and the F0 method described in the paper.

claim: More than 75% of disease-associated genes have an orthologue in the zebrafish genome.
source: Indeed, more than 75% of disease-associated genes have an orthologue in the zebrafish genome (Howe et al., 2013), optical translucence allows for whole brain imaging (Ahrens et al., 2013), and behavioural phenotypes can be robustly quantified early in development (Rihel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Howe et al., 2013.

claim: Optical translucence of zebrafish allows for whole brain imaging.
source: Indeed, more than 75% of disease-associated genes have an orthologue in the zebrafish genome (Howe et al., 2013), optical translucence allows for whole brain imaging (Ahrens et al., 2013), and behavioural phenotypes can be robustly quantified early in development (Rihel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ahrens et al., 2013.

claim: Behavioural phenotypes in zebrafish can be robustly quantified early in development.
source: Indeed, more than 75% of disease-associated genes have an orthologue in the zebrafish genome (Howe et al., 2013), optical translucence allows for whole brain imaging (Ahrens et al., 2013), and behavioural phenotypes can be robustly quantified early in development (Rihel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rihel et al., 2010.

claim: The pace at which new genetic associations are being identified currently far outstrips our ability to build a functional understanding in vivo.
source: However, the pace at which new genetic associations are being identified currently far outstrips our ability to build a functional understanding in vivo.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the field based on general knowledge.

claim: In zebrafish, a key limiting factor is the time and space needed to generate animals harbouring a mutation in the gene of interest.
source: In zebrafish, a key limiting factor is the time and space needed to generate animals harbouring a mutation in the gene of interest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' understanding of the limitations of current methods.

claim: Genome editing using CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionised our ability to generate zebrafish mutant lines.
source: Genome editing using CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionised our ability to generate zebrafish mutant lines (Hwang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hwang et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The common CRISPR-Cas9 strategy is to inject a Cas9/guide RNA (gRNA) ribonucleoprotein (RNP) into the single-cell embryo.
source: The common strategy is to inject a Cas9/guide RNA (gRNA) ribonucleoprotein (RNP) into the single-cell embryo (Sorlien et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sorlien et al., 2018.

claim: The gRNA binds to the targeted region of the genome and Cas9 produces a double-strand break.
source: The gRNA binds to the targeted region of the genome and Cas9 produces a double-strand break.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how CRISPR-Cas9 works.

claim: When joining the two ends after a Cas9-induced double-strand break, DNA repair mechanisms may introduce an indel by inserting or deleting bases in the target locus.
source: When joining the two ends, DNA repair mechanisms may introduce an indel by inserting or deleting bases in the target locus (Brinkman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brinkman et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: Indels often disrupt protein function, either by mutating sequences that encode essential residues or by introducing a frameshift that leads to a premature stop codon and a truncated, non-functional protein.
source: Indels often disrupt protein function, either by mutating sequences that encode essential residues or by introducing a frameshift that leads to a premature stop codon and a truncated, non-functional protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequences of indels on protein function.

claim: With CRISPR-Cas9, virtually any locus in the zebrafish genome can be disrupted.
source: With this tool, virtually any locus in the zebrafish genome can be disrupted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flexibility and targeting capability of CRISPR-Cas9 technology.

claim: Homozygous mutants using traditional CRISPR methods are only obtained after two generations of adult animals, which typically takes four to six months.
source: However, homozygous mutants are only obtained after two generations of adult animals, which typically takes four to six months (Sorlien et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sorlien et al., 2018.

claim: The traditional breeding bottleneck places substantial constraints on genetic screens in terms of time, costs, and ethical limits on animal numbers.
source: This bottleneck places substantial constraints on genetic screens in terms of time, costs, and ethical limits on animal numbers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the practical implications of the time required for traditional breeding methods.

claim: The main hurdle for F0 knockouts is to introduce a deleterious mutation in most or all copies of the genome without causing non-specific phenotypic consequences.
source: The main hurdle is to introduce a deleterious mutation in most or all copies of the genome without causing non-specific phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' understanding of the challenges in F0 knockout methodology.

claim: Meticulous optimisation of design, preparation, and delivery of the RNP has improved mutagenesis consistently enough to allow the successful use of zebrafish F0 knockouts in screens for visible developmental phenotypes.
source: Since the first applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo (Chang et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2013), meticulous optimisation of design (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015), preparation, and delivery of the RNP (Burger et al., 2016) has improved mutagenesis consistently enough to allow the successful use of zebrafish F0 knockouts in screens for visible developmental phenotypes, such as cardiac development (Wu et al., 2018), formation of electrical synapses (Shah et al., 2015), or distribution of microglia (Kuil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the progression of F0 knockout methodology.

claim: F0 knockouts have been successfully used in screens for cardiac development.
source: Since the first applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo (Chang et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2013), meticulous optimisation of design (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015), preparation, and delivery of the RNP (Burger et al., 2016) has improved mutagenesis consistently enough to allow the successful use of zebrafish F0 knockouts in screens for visible developmental phenotypes, such as cardiac development (Wu et al., 2018), formation of electrical synapses (Shah et al., 2015), or distribution of microglia (Kuil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2018.

claim: F0 knockouts have been successfully used in screens for formation of electrical synapses.
source: Since the first applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo (Chang et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2013), meticulous optimisation of design (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015), preparation, and delivery of the RNP (Burger et al., 2016) has improved mutagenesis consistently enough to allow the successful use of zebrafish F0 knockouts in screens for visible developmental phenotypes, such as cardiac development (Wu et al., 2018), formation of electrical synapses (Shah et al., 2015), or distribution of microglia (Kuil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2015.

claim: F0 knockouts have been successfully used in screens for distribution of microglia.
source: Since the first applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo (Chang et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2013), meticulous optimisation of design (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015), preparation, and delivery of the RNP (Burger et al., 2016) has improved mutagenesis consistently enough to allow the successful use of zebrafish F0 knockouts in screens for visible developmental phenotypes, such as cardiac development (Wu et al., 2018), formation of electrical synapses (Shah et al., 2015), or distribution of microglia (Kuil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuil et al., 2019.

claim: For visible developmental phenotypes, disrupting a single locus may be adequate as incomplete removal of wild-type alleles does not impair detection of the phenotype.
source: In these applications, disrupting a single locus may be adequate as incomplete removal of wild-type alleles does not impair detection of the phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of visible developmental phenotypes and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutants with an overt developmental defect can be identified even in heterogenous populations where some animals are not complete knockouts.
source: For example, mutants with an overt developmental defect can be identified even in heterogenous populations where some animals are not complete knockouts (Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burger et al., 2016.

claim: Certain phenotypes may be manifest in an animal in which only a subset of the cells carry mutant alleles.
source: Similarly, certain phenotypes may be manifest in an animal in which only a subset of the cells carry mutant alleles (Kuil et al., 2019; Shah et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuil et al., 2019 and Shah et al., 2015.

claim: Incomplete conversion into null alleles is potentially problematic when studying traits that vary continuously.
source: However, incomplete conversion into null alleles is potentially problematic when studying traits that vary continuously, especially if the spread of phenotypic values is already substantial in wild-type animals, which is regularly the case for behavioural parameters.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical considerations for detecting phenotypes in continuous traits.

claim: The spread of phenotypic values is regularly substantial in wild-type animals for behavioural parameters.
source: However, incomplete conversion into null alleles is potentially problematic when studying traits that vary continuously, especially if the spread of phenotypic values is already substantial in wild-type animals, which is regularly the case for behavioural parameters.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the variability of behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Animals in the experimental pool retaining variable levels of wild-type alleles will create overlap between the mutant and wild-type distributions of phenotypic values, reducing the likelihood of robustly distinguishing a mutant phenotype.
source: Animals in the experimental pool retaining variable levels of wild-type alleles will create overlap between the mutant and wild-type distributions of phenotypic values, reducing the likelihood of robustly distinguishing a mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical principles regarding the detection of phenotypic differences.

claim: An alternative strategy to ensure a high proportion of null alleles is to increase the probability of a frameshift by targeting the gene at multiple loci.
source: To ensure a high proportion of null alleles, an alternative strategy is to increase the probability of a frameshift by targeting the gene at multiple loci (Hoshijima et al., 2019; Sunagawa et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2014; Zuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting multi-locus targeting strategies.

claim: Rounds of DNA breaks and repair usually occur across multiple cell cycles.
source: Because rounds of DNA breaks and repair usually occur across multiple cell cycles (McKenna et al., 2016), different F0 animals, cells, or copies of the genome can harbour different null alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKenna et al., 2016.

claim: Different F0 animals, cells, or copies of the genome can harbour different null alleles.
source: Because rounds of DNA breaks and repair usually occur across multiple cell cycles (McKenna et al., 2016), different F0 animals, cells, or copies of the genome can harbour different null alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis and DNA repair.

claim: Targeting multiple loci inflates the diversity of alleles.
source: Targeting multiple loci inflates this diversity of alleles, which is perceived as a potential obstacle for rigorously describing complex phenotypes in F0 knockouts, particularly behavioural ones (Teboul et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combinatorial nature of mutations at multiple loci.

claim: Diversity of alleles is perceived as a potential obstacle for rigorously describing complex phenotypes in F0 knockouts, particularly behavioural ones.
source: Targeting multiple loci inflates this diversity of alleles, which is perceived as a potential obstacle for rigorously describing complex phenotypes in F0 knockouts, particularly behavioural ones (Teboul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teboul et al., 2017.

claim: The F0 knockout protocol uses a set of three synthetic gRNAs per gene.
source: The protocol uses a set of three synthetic gRNAs per gene, combining multi-locus targeting with high mutagenesis at each locus.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in the study.

claim: The F0 knockout method combines multi-locus targeting with high mutagenesis at each locus.
source: The protocol uses a set of three synthetic gRNAs per gene, combining multi-locus targeting with high mutagenesis at each locus.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in the study.

claim: The F0 knockout method consistently converts > 90% of injected embryos into biallelic knockouts that show fully penetrant pigmentation phenotypes.
source: The method consistently converts > 90% of injected embryos into biallelic knockouts that show fully penetrant pigmentation phenotypes and near complete absence of wild-type alleles in deep sequencing data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The F0 knockout method consistently converts > 90% of injected embryos into biallelic knockouts that show near complete absence of wild-type alleles in deep sequencing data.
source: The method consistently converts > 90% of injected embryos into biallelic knockouts that show fully penetrant pigmentation phenotypes and near complete absence of wild-type alleles in deep sequencing data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The authors developed a quick and cheap PCR-based tool to validate gRNAs.
source: In parallel, we developed a quick and cheap PCR-based tool to validate gRNAs whatever the nature of the mutant alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The PCR-based validation tool works whatever the nature of the mutant alleles.
source: In parallel, we developed a quick and cheap PCR-based tool to validate gRNAs whatever the nature of the mutant alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing the tool works for various types of mutations.

claim: The F0 knockout protocol is easily adapted to generate biallelic mutations in up to three genes in individual animals.
source: The F0 knockout protocol is easily adapted to generate biallelic mutations in up to three genes in individual animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing double and triple gene knockouts.

claim: The populations of F0 knockout animals generated by the method are suitable for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes.
source: The populations of F0 knockout animals generated by the method are suitable for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes, as demonstrated by mutation of a circadian clock component and by meticulous replication of multi-parameter behavioural phenotypes of a genetic model of epilepsy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mutation of a circadian clock component in F0 knockouts demonstrates suitability for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes.
source: The populations of F0 knockout animals generated by the method are suitable for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes, as demonstrated by mutation of a circadian clock component and by meticulous replication of multi-parameter behavioural phenotypes of a genetic model of epilepsy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B showing csnk1db F0 knockout circadian phenotypes.

claim: Meticulous replication of multi-parameter behavioural phenotypes of a genetic model of epilepsy in F0 knockouts demonstrates suitability for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes.
source: The populations of F0 knockout animals generated by the method are suitable for quantitative analysis of complex phenotypes, as demonstrated by mutation of a circadian clock component and by meticulous replication of multi-parameter behavioural phenotypes of a genetic model of epilepsy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing scn1lab F0 knockout behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Using standard genetic approaches, the gap from gene to behavioural phenotype in zebrafish often takes half a year.
source: Using standard genetic approaches, the gap from gene to behavioural phenotype in zebrafish often takes half a year.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the time required for traditional breeding methods.

claim: The F0 knockout method enables obtaining behavioral phenotypes in a week.
source: Our F0 knockout method enables this in a week.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental timeline of the F0 knockout method.

claim: These methodological improvements will greatly facilitate the use of zebrafish to tackle genetic questions in neuroscience.
source: We believe these methodological improvements will greatly facilitate the use of zebrafish to tackle genetic questions in neuroscience, such as those addressing the contributions of disease-associated genes to nervous system development, circuit function, and behaviour.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the method.

claim: Targeting slc24a5 with three RNPs generated 95% (55/58) of larvae totally devoid of eye pigmentation.
source: Conversely, when three RNPs were injected, 95% (55/58) of larvae were totally devoid of eye pigmentation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Using just two RNPs to target tyr yielded 59/59 F0 embryos with no eye pigmentation.
source: For example, using just two RNPs to target tyr yielded 59/59 F0 embryos with no eye pigmentation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Adding a fourth RNP to slc24a5 targeting did not increase the phenotypic penetrance further beyond three RNPs.
source: Adding a fourth RNP did not increase the penetrance further.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C comparing three and four RNPs.

claim: The number of unviable embryos increased when targeting a fourth locus.
source: In both experiments, the number of unviable embryos remained at tolerable levels but increased when targeting a fourth locus (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Injecting a pre-assembled Cas9 protein/gRNA RNP is more mutagenic in zebrafish than co-injecting Cas9 mRNA and gRNA.
source: Injecting a pre-assembled Cas9 protein/gRNA RNP is more mutagenic in zebrafish than co-injecting Cas9 mRNA and gRNA (Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burger et al., 2016.

claim: For both slc24a5 and tyr, more Cas9 resulted in more larvae without any eye pigmentation.
source: For both slc24a5 and tyr, more Cas9 resulted in more larvae without any eye pigmentation, implying that Cas9 should be present at the 1-to-1 ratio with gRNA or even in excess for optimal results (at the 1-to-1 ratio, 63/67 slc24a5 and 71/74 tyr F0 larvae lacked eye pigmentation) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the 1-to-1 Cas9:gRNA ratio, 63/67 slc24a5 F0 larvae lacked eye pigmentation.
source: For both slc24a5 and tyr, more Cas9 resulted in more larvae without any eye pigmentation, implying that Cas9 should be present at the 1-to-1 ratio with gRNA or even in excess for optimal results (at the 1-to-1 ratio, 63/67 slc24a5 and 71/74 tyr F0 larvae lacked eye pigmentation) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: At the 1-to-1 Cas9:gRNA ratio, 71/74 tyr F0 larvae lacked eye pigmentation.
source: For both slc24a5 and tyr, more Cas9 resulted in more larvae without any eye pigmentation, implying that Cas9 should be present at the 1-to-1 ratio with gRNA or even in excess for optimal results (at the 1-to-1 ratio, 63/67 slc24a5 and 71/74 tyr F0 larvae lacked eye pigmentation) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: All (41/41) adult slc24a5 F0 fish still displayed the golden phenotype at 2.5 months.
source: All (41/41) adult slc24a5 F0 fish still displayed the golden phenotype (Lamason et al., 2005) at 2.5 months (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Incrossing the slc24a5 F0 adult fish produced clutches of embryos that were all devoid of eye pigmentation at 2 dpf (n = 3 clutches, total 283/283 embryos).
source: Incrossing the slc24a5 F0 adult fish produced clutches of embryos that were all devoid of eye pigmentation at 2 dpf (n = 3 clutches, total 283/283 embryos), while outcrossing them to wild types produced larvae displaying wild-type pigmentation (n = 3 clutches, total 313/313 embryos) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Outcrossing slc24a5 F0 adult fish to wild types produced larvae displaying wild-type pigmentation (n = 3 clutches, total 313/313 embryos).
source: Incrossing the slc24a5 F0 adult fish produced clutches of embryos that were all devoid of eye pigmentation at 2 dpf (n = 3 clutches, total 283/283 embryos), while outcrossing them to wild types produced larvae displaying wild-type pigmentation (n = 3 clutches, total 313/313 embryos) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: The F0 protocol directly produced phenotypically homozygous knockout animals without the need for breeding.
source: The F0 protocol thus directly produced phenotypically homozygous knockout animals without the need for breeding, and the mutations were transmitted through the germline.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing phenotypic penetrance and germline transmission.

claim: The mutations in F0 knockouts were transmitted through the germline.
source: The F0 protocol thus directly produced phenotypically homozygous knockout animals without the need for breeding, and the mutations were transmitted through the germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that F0 adults produced mutant offspring.

claim: 96% (96/100) of larvae injected with three RNPs targeting mab21l2 showed the microphthalmia phenotype.
source: 96% (96/100) of larvae injected with three RNPs targeting mab21l2 showed this phenotype (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1I.

claim: Homozygous mab21l2u517 mutants showed microphthalmia (small eye) with a flattened retina.
source: Homozygous mab21l2u517 (Wycliffe et al., 2020) mutants showed microphthalmia (small eye) with a flattened retina, resembling eye defects observed in humans with mutations in its ortholog MAB21L2 (Rainger et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wycliffe et al., 2020 and Rainger et al., 2014.

claim: 100% (93/93) of larvae injected with RNPs targeting tbx16 were evident spadetail mutants.
source: 100% (93/93) of the injected larvae were evident spadetail mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homozygous tbx16 loss-of-function mutants display the spadetail phenotype, characterised by a bent tail terminating in a clump of cells.
source: Homozygous tbx16 loss-of-function mutants display the spadetail phenotype, characterised by a bent tail terminating in a clump of cells (Ho and Kane, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ho and Kane, 1990.

claim: At each targeted locus, 87 ± 18% of the reads were mutated.
source: At each locus, 87 ± 18% of the reads were mutated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: If a read was mutated, the mean probability that it also carried a frameshift mutation was 65.4%.
source: If a read was mutated, the mean probability that it also carried a frameshift mutation was 65.4%, confirming the absence of bias in frameshift probability (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015) and verifying the assumption of the theoretical model that 2 out of every 3 mutations induce a frameshift.
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data analysis and confirms a theoretical prediction.

claim: The same RNP produced the same mutations in different animals more often than expected by chance.
source: The same RNP produced the same mutations in different animals more often than expected by chance (Figure 2B; two animals injected with the same RNP shared 3.3 ± 1.6 of their top 10 most frequent indels vs 0.5 ± 0.7 if they were injected with different RNPs), in line with a non-random outcome of DNA repair at Cas9 breaks (Shen et al., 2018; van Overbeek et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 2B and citations to previous work.

claim: Two animals injected with the same RNP shared 3.3 ± 1.6 of their top 10 most frequent indels vs 0.5 ± 0.7 if they were injected with different RNPs.
source: The same RNP produced the same mutations in different animals more often than expected by chance (Figure 2B; two animals injected with the same RNP shared 3.3 ± 1.6 of their top 10 most frequent indels vs 0.5 ± 0.7 if they were injected with different RNPs), in line with a non-random outcome of DNA repair at Cas9 breaks (Shen et al., 2018; van Overbeek et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis.

claim: Shorter indels were observed more often than longer ones.
source: As expected (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015; Varshney et al., 2015), shorter indels were observed more often than longer ones, with an overall bias towards deletions (Figure 2C; 57% deletions vs 43% insertions, n = 7015 unique indels).
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 2C and citations to previous work.

claim: There was an overall bias towards deletions (57% deletions vs 43% insertions, n = 7015 unique indels).
source: As expected (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015; Varshney et al., 2015), shorter indels were observed more often than longer ones, with an overall bias towards deletions (Figure 2C; 57% deletions vs 43% insertions, n = 7015 unique indels).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis.

claim: The positions of the deleted nucleotides are normally distributed with a peak at 4 bp before the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
source: The positions of the deleted nucleotides are normally distributed with a peak at 4 bp before the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming previous reports (Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to previous work.

claim: At each targeted locus, there were 40.5 ± 27.5 (median ± median absolute deviation) different alleles.
source: The diversity of null alleles in individual F0 knockout animals was extensive: at each targeted locus, there were 40.5 ± 27.5 (median ± median absolute deviation) different alleles, which in theory can produce up to hundreds of thousands of different versions of the targeted gene.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis.

claim: For all genes targeted (n = 10) and 31/35 of individual animals sequenced, three RNPs were sufficient to achieve over 80% of alleles harbouring a frameshift mutation.
source: For all genes targeted (n = 10) and 31/35 of individual animals sequenced, three RNPs were sufficient to achieve over 80% of alleles harbouring a frameshift mutation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 2D.

claim: For slc24a5, the fourth RNP only marginally augmented the proportion of frameshift alleles (+ 2.7%).
source: For slc24a5 and tyr, the fourth RNP only marginally augmented this proportion (+ 2.7% for slc24a5; + 4% for tyr) (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 1E.

claim: For tyr, the fourth RNP only marginally augmented the proportion of frameshift alleles (+ 4%).
source: For slc24a5 and tyr, the fourth RNP only marginally augmented this proportion (+ 2.7% for slc24a5; + 4% for tyr) (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The proportion of alleles harbouring a frameshift mutation is not sufficient alone to generate the high phenotypic penetrance observed.
source: Introducing a frameshift is a robust, widely applicable strategy to prevent the production of the protein of interest. However, the proportion of alleles harbouring a frameshift mutation is not sufficient alone to generate the high phenotypic penetrance we observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing sequencing data with phenotypic penetrance data.

claim: Of the larvae injected with three RNPs targeting slc24a5 or tyr, 3/6 had less than 90% alleles with a frameshift mutation, but phenotypic penetrance was consistently > 94%.
source: For example, of the larvae injected with three RNPs targeting slc24a5 or tyr, 3/6 had less than 90% alleles with a frameshift mutation (Figure 1E,F), but phenotypic penetrance was consistently > 94% (score 1 in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing sequencing data with phenotypic data.

claim: Mutations of residues at key domains of the protein can be sufficient for loss of function.
source: First, mutations of residues at key domains of the protein can be sufficient for loss of function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about protein function.

claim: Large indels may disrupt the sequencing PCR primers' binding sites, preventing amplification of such alleles.
source: Second, large indels may disrupt the sequencing PCR primers' binding sites, preventing amplification of such alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of PCR amplification.

claim: The pooled RNPs may lead to deletion of large sequences that span two loci being targeted.
source: Third, the pooled RNPs may also lead to deletion of large sequences that span two loci being targeted (Hoshijima et al., 2019; Kim and Zhang, 2020; Moreno-Mateos et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is confirmed by Sanger sequencing data in Figure 2E.

claim: Clear instances of large deletions between two targeted sites within slc24a5 were identified by Sanger sequencing.
source: To test the latter possibility, we Sanger sequenced amplicons from regions that span multiple targeted loci within slc24a5. We identified clear instances where the gene underwent a large deletion between two targeted sites (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Sanger sequencing data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Large deletions are highly likely to prevent the expression of a functional protein.
source: As large deletions are highly likely to prevent the expression of a functional protein, they further affirm the efficacy of the three-RNP strategy.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the consequences of large deletions on protein function.

claim: There were essentially no mutated reads (< 0.5%) at all but one off-target for slc24a5 gRNAs.
source: There were essentially no mutated reads (< 0.5%) at all but one off-target, for which mutated reads ranged between 15–54% (n = 4 larvae) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data of off-target sites presented in Figure 2F.

claim: For one off-target of slc24a5 gRNAs, mutated reads ranged between 15–54% (n = 4 larvae).
source: There were essentially no mutated reads (< 0.5%) at all but one off-target, for which mutated reads ranged between 15–54% (n = 4 larvae) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data of off-target sites presented in Figure 2F.

claim: 3/4 larvae had few or no reads with a frameshift mutation at the mutated off-target site (0%, 0%, 1.8%), while the fourth had 42% reads with a frameshift mutation.
source: Importantly, 3/4 larvae had few or no reads with a frameshift mutation at this site (0%, 0%, 1.8%), while the fourth had 42% reads with a frameshift mutation.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by deep sequencing data analysis.

claim: The mutated off-target had the lowest number of mismatches with the gRNA binding sequence (2 mismatches vs 3–4 for the other 8 off-target loci).
source: Of the 9 off-targets, the mutated off-target had the lowest number of mismatches with the gRNA binding sequence (2 mismatches vs 3–4 for the other 8 off-target loci) and the worst off-target risk (predicted score of 58 vs 59–87 for the other 8 off-target loci), indicating that mutations may be relatively predictable.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the off-target sequences and their predicted scores.

claim: Mutations at off-targets may be relatively predictable based on sequence mismatches and predicted scores.
source: Of the 9 off-targets, the mutated off-target had the lowest number of mismatches with the gRNA binding sequence (2 mismatches vs 3–4 for the other 8 off-target loci) and the worst off-target risk (predicted score of 58 vs 59–87 for the other 8 off-target loci), indicating that mutations may be relatively predictable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between predicted off-target scores and observed mutations.

claim: Mutations at off-targets are unlikely to be sufficient to produce consistently high proportions of biallelic null alleles.
source: These levels of mutagenesis at a single locus are unlikely to be sufficient to produce consistently high proportions of biallelic null alleles, either in individual animals or at the level of the population of F0 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of off-target mutagenesis levels with on-target levels.

claim: Mutations at off-targets are not considered a major concern in applications where a population of F0 knockout animals is phenotyped.
source: Hence, we do not consider mutations at off-targets to be a major concern in applications where a population of F0 knockout animals is phenotyped.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of off-target mutation data.

claim: The simple protocol involving three synthetic RNPs at 1:1 Cas9 to gRNA ratio takes just a few hours to complete.
source: Overall, our simple protocol involving three synthetic RNPs at 1:1 Cas9 to gRNA ratio takes just a few hours to complete yet consistently achieves > 90% biallelic knockouts.
evidence: This is a description of the practical aspects of the method.

claim: The method generates a diverse mix of null alleles in the injected animals.
source: While the method generates a diverse mix of null alleles in the injected animals, frameshift mutations are a universal mechanism which can be deployed on virtually any gene of interest.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the deep sequencing data showing allele diversity.

claim: Frameshift mutations are a universal mechanism which can be deployed on virtually any gene of interest.
source: While the method generates a diverse mix of null alleles in the injected animals, frameshift mutations are a universal mechanism which can be deployed on virtually any gene of interest.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about frameshift mutations and the flexibility of CRISPR-Cas9 targeting.

claim: Deep sequencing allows for the quantification of frameshift mutations in F0 animals, but the cost is not always justified simply to confirm sufficient mutagenic activity of gRNAs.
source: Deep sequencing allows for the quantification of frameshift mutations in F0 animals, but the cost is not always justified simply to confirm sufficient mutagenic activity of gRNAs.
evidence: This is a practical consideration based on the cost-benefit analysis of sequencing.

claim: The authors adapted a suppression PCR method called headloop PCR.
source: As an inexpensive and rapid alternative, we adapted a suppression PCR method called headloop PCR (Rand et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rand et al., 2005 and experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Suppression in headloop PCR is achieved by adding to one of the PCR primers a 5' tag that is complementary to the wild-type sequence at the target locus.
source: Suppression is achieved by adding to one of the PCR primers a 5' tag that is complementary to the wild-type sequence at the target locus.
evidence: This is a description of the headloop PCR method.

claim: During PCR, the headloop tag base-pairs to the target sequence in the same strand, directing elongation to form a stable hairpin, which prevents the use of the amplicon as template in the subsequent cycles.
source: During PCR, the tag base-pairs to the target sequence in the same strand, directing elongation to form a stable hairpin, which prevents the use of the amplicon as template in the subsequent cycles (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of headloop PCR illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Any indels generated in the target locus will prevent the formation of the headloop and allow exponential amplification.
source: Any indels generated in the target locus will prevent the formation of the headloop and allow exponential amplification.
evidence: This is a description of how headloop PCR detects mutations.

claim: No amplification with headloop primers was detected for any of the loci in uninjected embryos, indicating suppression of amplification of the wild-type haplotype.
source: No amplification with headloop primers was detected for any of the loci in uninjected embryos, indicating suppression of amplification of the wild-type haplotype (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Robust amplification of the targeted loci was observed from the F0 embryos injected with highly mutagenic RNPs.
source: In contrast, robust amplification of the targeted loci was observed from the F0 embryos injected with highly mutagenic RNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: Amplification was absent at the locus targeted by a gRNA known to be ineffective (slc24a5 gRNA C, < 2% mutated reads).
source: Amplification was absent at the locus targeted by a gRNA known to be ineffective (slc24a5 gRNA C, < 2% mutated reads; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing correlation between headloop PCR results and sequencing data.

claim: The headloop score correlated well with the proportion of mutated reads measured by deep sequencing (r = 0.66, n = 29 samples tested from n = 7 loci).
source: This score correlated well with the proportion of mutated reads measured by deep sequencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; r = 0.66, n = 29 samples tested from n = 7 loci).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A tentative headloop score threshold at 0.6 could discriminate gRNAs that were less mutagenic.
source: A tentative headloop score threshold at 0.6 could discriminate gRNAs that were less mutagenic (tbx16 gRNA B and tyr gRNA A, both generated < 60% mutated reads).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between headloop scores and sequencing data.

claim: Headloop PCR can be used in a semi-quantitative manner to confirm that mutagenesis is high at every targeted site, although it may at times be overly conservative.
source: We conclude that headloop PCR can be used in a semi-quantitative manner to confirm that mutagenesis is high at every targeted site, although it may at times be overly conservative.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental validation of headloop PCR.

claim: Sanger sequencing corroborated 100% of the genotype calls made by headloop PCR for two stable mutant lines.
source: Sanger sequencing corroborated 100% of the genotype calls made by headloop PCR.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Small deletions (1-2 bp) are sufficient to prevent the formation of the hairpin in headloop PCR.
source: Small deletions are therefore sufficient to prevent the formation of the hairpin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing headloop PCR can detect small deletions.

claim: Use of a proofreading polymerase (with 3′→5′ exonuclease activity) was essential for effective suppression in headloop PCR.
source: Importantly, we determined that use of a proofreading polymerase (with 3′→5′ exonuclease activity) was essential for effective suppression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), presumably because replication errors made in the target sequence prevent the formation of the hairpin.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The adapted headloop PCR method is a simple, sensitive, inexpensive, and rapid approach to verify the mutagenic potential of gRNAs before undertaking an F0 phenotypic screen.
source: These results demonstrate that our adapted headloop PCR method is a simple, sensitive, inexpensive, and rapid approach to verify the mutagenic potential of gRNAs before undertaking an F0 phenotypic screen.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental validation of the headloop PCR method.

claim: When both slc24a5 and tbx5a were targeted in individual animals, 93% (26/28) displayed both phenotypes.
source: When both genes were targeted in individual animals, 93% (26/28) displayed both phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: 100% of the embryos injected with RNPs targeting both tyr and ta exhibited both the no pigmentation and no tail phenotypes.
source: 100% of the injected embryos exhibited both the no pigmentation and no tail phenotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: These experiments demonstrate the feasibility of simultaneously disrupting two genes directly in the F0 animals.
source: These experiments demonstrate the feasibility of simultaneously disrupting two genes directly in the F0 animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the double knockout experimental data.

claim: 9/10 of viable larvae injected with RNPs targeting slc45a2, mitfa, and mpv17 displayed the transparent crystal phenotype.
source: Nonetheless, 9/10 of viable larvae displayed the transparent crystal phenotype (Figure 4C left).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Targeting three genes simultaneously lowered viability by 4 dpf (50% of injected larvae were unviable).
source: Targeting three genes simultaneously lowered viability by 4 dpf (50% of injected larvae were unviable).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: The crystal F0 larvae expressing pan-neuronal GCaMP6s were suitable for live imaging under a two-photon microscope.
source: The crystal F0 larvae expressing pan-neuronal GCaMP6s were suitable for live imaging under a two-photon microscope.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4C and associated videos.

claim: The whole brain and the eyes could be effectively imaged in vivo at single-cell resolution in crystal F0 larvae.
source: The whole brain and the eyes could be effectively imaged in vivo at single-cell resolution (Figure 4C right, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4C and associated videos.

claim: Amacrine and ganglion cells in the retina could be imaged in crystal F0 larvae, which are not normally accessible to imaging in other single-gene knockout lines routinely used for imaging, such as nacre.
source: This included amacrine and ganglion cells in the retina, which are not normally accessible to imaging in other single-gene knockout lines routinely used for imaging, such as nacre (Lister et al., 1999), due to persistence of pigments in the retinal pigment epithelium (Antinucci and Hindges, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and citations to previous work.

claim: The F0 knockout protocol rapidly produced crystal larvae directly in a transgenic line without the need for crossing.
source: The F0 knockout protocol rapidly produced crystal larvae directly in a transgenic line without the need for crossing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the triple knockout experimental data.

claim: trpa1b encodes an ion channel implicated in behavioural responses to chemical irritants such as mustard oil (allyl isothiocyanate).
source: trpa1b encodes an ion channel implicated in behavioural responses to chemical irritants such as mustard oil (allyl isothiocyanate).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of trpa1b.

claim: Wild-type larvae show a robust escape response when exposed to mustard oil, while trpa1bvu197 null mutants do not react strongly.
source: While wild-type larvae show a robust escape response when exposed to this compound, trpa1bvu197 null mutants do not react strongly (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prober et al., 2008.

claim: Most (19/22) trpa1b F0 knockout larvae failed to strongly respond to mustard oil.
source: While scrambled-injected control larvae displayed an escape response when mustard oil was added to the water, most (19/22) trpa1b F0 knockout larvae failed to strongly respond (Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: trpa1b F0 knockouts replicated the established stable trpa1bvu197 loss-of-function mutant behavioural phenotype.
source: Therefore, trpa1b F0 knockouts replicated the established stable trpa1bvu197 loss-of-function mutant behavioural phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of F0 knockout behavior with published mutant phenotypes.

claim: The circadian period of control larvae injected with scrambled RNPs in constant dark conditions was 25.8 ± 0.9 hr.
source: The circadian period of control larvae injected with scrambled RNPs in constant dark conditions was 25.8 ± 0.9 hr, within the expected wild-type range (Kaneko and Cahill, 2005).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: In csnk1db F0 knockout animals, the circadian period was extended by 84 min to 27.2 ± 0.9 hr.
source: In csnk1db F0 knockout animals, the circadian period was extended by 84 min to 27.2 ± 0.9 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: When PF-670462 was added to scrambled RNPs-injected larvae, the period increased more than 8 hr to 34.1 ± 0.9 hr.
source: When PF-670462 was added to scrambled RNPs-injected larvae, the period increased more than 8 hr to 34.1 ± 0.9 hr.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Adding PF-670462 to the csnk1db F0 larvae did not further increase the period (34.3 ± 2.7 hr).
source: However, adding the inhibitor to the csnk1db F0 larvae did not further increase the period (34.3 ± 2.7 hr).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The phenotypic consequences of the casein-kinase inhibitor and csnk1db knockout are not additive, indicating that they influence circadian period length through the same target pathway.
source: Therefore, the phenotypic consequences of the casein-kinase inhibitor and csnk1db knockout are not additive, indicating that they influence circadian period length through the same target pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no additive effect.

claim: A quantitative molecular phenotype that unfolds over many days and in many tissues can be accurately detected in the population of F0 knockouts generated with the protocol.
source: This experiment demonstrates that a quantitative molecular phenotype that unfolds over many days and in many tissues can be accurately detected in the population of F0 knockouts generated with our protocol.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the csnk1db circadian rhythm experimental data.

claim: scn1lab encodes a sodium channel.
source: To test this, we targeted scn1lab, which encodes a sodium channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gene scn1lab.

claim: In humans, loss-of-function mutations of SCN1A (ortholog of scn1lab) are associated with Dravet syndrome, a rare and intractable childhood epilepsy.
source: In humans, loss-of-function mutations of its ortholog SCN1A are associated with Dravet syndrome, a rare and intractable childhood epilepsy (Anwar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anwar et al., 2019.

claim: In zebrafish, scn1lab homozygous null mutants display hyperpigmentation, seizures, and complex day-night differences in free-swimming behaviour.
source: In zebrafish, scn1lab homozygous null mutants display hyperpigmentation, seizures, and complex day-night differences in free-swimming behaviour (Baraban et al., 2013; Grone et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baraban et al., 2013 and Grone et al., 2017.

claim: All (91/91) scn1lab F0 knockouts were hyperpigmented.
source: As expected, all (91/91) scn1lab F0 knockouts were hyperpigmented (Figure 6A insert).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygous null mutants had similar behavioural changes compared to their wild-type siblings.
source: F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygous null mutants had similar behavioural changes compared to their wild-type siblings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: During the day, both F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygotes spent less time active compared to wild types (all three experiments p < 0.001 by two-way ANOVA).
source: During the day, both F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygotes spent less time active compared to wild types (all three experiments p < 0.001 by two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: At night, F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygotes were as active as wild types initially, then showed a gradual ramping to hyperactivity.
source: At night, F0 knockouts and scn1labΔ44 homozygotes were as active as wild types initially, then showed a gradual ramping to hyperactivity (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two clutches of scn1lab F0 knockouts had highly correlated behavioural fingerprints (r = 0.89).
source: The two clutches of scn1lab F0 knockouts had highly correlated behavioural fingerprints (r = 0.89), and each correlated well with the fingerprint of the scn1labΔ44 homozygotes (r = 0.86, r = 0.75).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Each scn1lab F0 knockout clutch correlated well with the fingerprint of the scn1labΔ44 homozygotes (r = 0.86, r = 0.75).
source: The two clutches of scn1lab F0 knockouts had highly correlated behavioural fingerprints (r = 0.89), and each correlated well with the fingerprint of the scn1labΔ44 homozygotes (r = 0.86, r = 0.75).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: scn1labΔ44 homozygotes and both scn1lab F0 knockout clutches were significantly distant from their wild-type counterparts in Euclidean distance analysis.
source: Unlike scn1labΔ44 heterozygous larvae, which do not display overt phenotypes, scn1labΔ44 homozygotes and both scn1lab F0 knockout clutches were significantly distant from their wild-type counterparts (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Diversity of null alleles is not a barrier to measuring detailed mutant behavioural phenotypes in populations of F0 knockouts.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that diversity of null alleles is not a barrier to measuring detailed mutant behavioural phenotypes in populations of F0 knockouts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the scn1lab behavioral experimental data.

claim: Complex continuous traits, including behavioural phenotypes, can be rigorously measured directly in F0 animals.
source: In summary, complex continuous traits, including behavioural phenotypes, can be rigorously measured directly in F0 animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the phenotyping experiments (trpa1b, csnk1db, scn1lab).

claim: A single 96-well plate (sample sizes of 48 larvae in each group) is more than sufficient to detect mutant phenotypes at a power of 0.8 and a significance level of 0.05, even with a relatively low proportion of knockout animals in the F0 population.
source: Power calculations on simulations derived from the trpa1b and csnk1db F0 knockout experimental data show that a single 96-well plate, i.e. sample sizes of 48 larvae in each group, is more than sufficient to detect mutant phenotypes at a power of 0.8 and a significance level of 0.05, even with a relatively low proportion of knockout animals in the F0 population (28 and 59%, respectively; Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by power analysis simulations presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The high efficacy and throughput of the F0 method allows one to discover phenotypes with robust statistical power.
source: Therefore, the high efficacy and throughput of the F0 method allows one to discover phenotypes with robust statistical power.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the power analysis simulations.

claim: A key characteristic of the F0 knockout approach is the diversity of null alleles.
source: A key characteristic of the F0 knockout approach is the diversity of null alleles.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the F0 knockout method based on the sequencing data.

claim: The F0 mutants do not have a unique, definable genotype.
source: The F0 mutants do not have a unique, definable genotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the deep sequencing data showing allele diversity.

claim: In a survey of 193 knockout lines in HAP1 cells, around one third still produced residual levels of the target protein, thanks in part to genetic compensatory mechanisms such as skipping of the mutated exon or translation from alternative start codons.
source: For example, in a survey of 193 knockout lines in HAP1 cells, around one third still produced residual levels of the target protein, thanks in part to genetic compensatory mechanisms such as skipping of the mutated exon or translation from alternative start codons (Smits et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smits et al., 2019.

claim: Exon skipping has been documented in stable zebrafish knockout lines.
source: Exon skipping has also been documented in stable zebrafish knockout lines (Anderson et al., 2017; Lalonde et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017 and Lalonde et al., 2017.

claim: By creating a diverse array of mutations at three sites per gene, each on a separate exon wherever possible, compensatory mechanisms are not likely to allow the production of a functional protein in the F0 knockouts.
source: By creating a diverse array of mutations at three sites per gene, each on a separate exon wherever possible, such compensatory mechanisms are not likely to allow the production of a functional protein in the F0 knockouts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multi-locus targeting strategy and knowledge of compensatory mechanisms.

claim: A given phenotype may differ between different null alleles.
source: Furthermore, a given phenotype may differ between different null alleles (Chiavacci et al., 2017; Schuermann et al., 2015) or between different genetic backgrounds (Garrity et al., 2002; Sanders and Whitlock, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiavacci et al., 2017 and Schuermann et al., 2015.

claim: A given phenotype may differ between different genetic backgrounds.
source: Furthermore, a given phenotype may differ between different null alleles (Chiavacci et al., 2017; Schuermann et al., 2015) or between different genetic backgrounds (Garrity et al., 2002; Sanders and Whitlock, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garrity et al., 2002 and Sanders and Whitlock, 2003.

claim: A knockout phenotype detected in a genetically diverse population of F0 animals is likely to be a robust and reproducible description of the impact caused by the absence of the protein.
source: Accordingly, we propose that a knockout phenotype detected in this genetically diverse population of animals is likely to be a robust and reproducible description of the impact caused by the absence of the protein, akin to reaching a synthesised conclusion after comparing stable knockout lines of different alleles and from different founder animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the advantages of the F0 approach.
